lesson.title: Static Routes: When You Tell the Router Exactly What to Do
lesson.summary: A static route is a routing table entry an administrator configures by hand, one that stays fixed until someone changes or removes it, rather than being learned automatically.
lesson.body:
Every entry in a routing table has to come from somewhere. Sometimes that source is an administrator sitting at a keyboard, typing in a command that says, in effect, to reach this network, send traffic to that next hop. This manually configured entry is a static route. It is the simplest possible way to populate a routing table: no protocol runs, no messages are exchanged with neighboring routers, and the entry does not change on its own, no matter what happens elsewhere in the network.

That simplicity is both the appeal and the limitation. Consider a small office with exactly one router and one connection to the outside world through a single upstream provider. There is only ever one sensible way out, so an administrator can add a single static route, for example a route to network 0.0.0.0/0, a pattern we will look at closely in the next chapter, with a next hop pointing at the provider's router, and be done. The route uses no CPU cycles recalculating paths, sends no update traffic, and behaves in a perfectly predictable way, which matters in networks where predictability and easy troubleshooting are worth more than automatic adaptability.

The tradeoff shows up the moment the network gets more complex or less reliable. A static route has no way to notice that its next hop has gone down, it will happily keep pointing traffic at a dead link until a human notices and fixes it. In a network with multiple possible paths, redundant links, or frequent changes, that rigidity becomes a real liability, which is exactly the gap that dynamic routing algorithms, like the distance vector approach covered later in this chapter, are built to fill. Static routes remain useful even in dynamic networks, though, for cases like a defined backup path, a route to a network too small or specific to advertise, or, most commonly, the default route covered next.
